newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia GDP shows first post-reform quarterly growth.
newsitem.headline: Russia GDP shows first post-reform quarterly growth.

text.p: Russia's economy has recorded its first quarterly growth since the break-up of the Soviet Union in 1991, according to government figures released on Monday.
But some economists said recent controversial changes in the way the numbers are calculated raise doubts over whether the data give a true picture of the economy.
"The great decline in the Russian economy over the last decade has practically ended," Chairman of the State Statistics Committee Yuri Yurkov told a news conference.
Figures released by the committee showed gross domestic product in the first quarter of 1997 was 0.2 percent higher than a year earlier -- the first growth after seven years of plummeting output.
By the end of 1996 the economy was only 61 percent of its size when the Soviet Union broke up and reforms began, a level last seen in 1979.
But some analysts do not trust the new figures.

"The Russian economy is a bit blind, it's not clear what total revenues are as well as other key indicators needed to analyse the economy overall," said Vladimir Gurevich, Deputy Editor in Chief of Moscow News.

Critics said the quarterly figures were as suspect as the rosy industrial production and GDP figures for the beginning of the year, which were achieved by increasing the weight of the thriving shadow economy.
"My impression is that they are over-representing what's going on, said Roland Nash, chief economist at Moscow investment bank Renaissance Capital.
The committee said the shadow economy made up about 23 percent of GDP at the beginning of the year. Earlier calculations gave it a 20 percent weighting.
Consumer price inflation in the first quarter slowed to a post-reform low of 16.7 percent over the same period in 1996.
Yurkov said the positive GDP and industrial production figures did not mean the economy was now growing.
Some economists said the underlying trend was stable, although published 1997 growth rates could come down if last year's indicators are revised for the shadow economy.
The Russian government has predicted 2 percent growth this year, but some economists say growth may not resume until 1998.
